full_judgment:
4. The plaintiffs' case, in short, is that the land of the original C.S. Khatian No.42, C.S. Plot No.45 comprising an area of 1.75 acres originally belonged to Sabjan Bibi. Sabjan Bibi sold the same land to Lal Mohammad and in the C.S. Khatian, Lal Mohammad's name was recorded correctly in the possession column as "possession by purchase". While in possession, Lal Mohammad died leaving behind 5 sons, namely, Dhanu Miah, Tamijuddin, Kamaruddin, Janab Ali and Samad Ali as his heirs. These 5(five) brothers were owning and possessing the suit property in ejmali. Subsequently, the said 5(five) brothers made amicable partition of their ejmali landed property among themselves and according to that amicable partition they were owning and possessing their respective share. Kamaruddin died leaving behind 2(two) sons Sultan and Ashraf Ali and widow Gulmeher Bibi who were owning and possessing .27 acre of land as heirs of Kamaruddin. They sold the said .27 acre of land to one Sabu Miah by a registered deed dated 22.10.1956. While owning and possessing that .27 acre land of the suit plot, Sabu Miah died leaving behind Kutu Miah, Badsha Miah and Sirajuddin as his heirs. Samad Ali, another son of Lal Mohammad, died leaving behind only son Faijuddin and said Faijuddin sold out his .27 acre land to Kutu Miah, Badsha Miah and Sirajuddin by registered sale deed dated16.08.1957. Thus Kutu Miah, Badsha Miah and Sirajuddin became owners of .54 acre land of the suit plot. While owning and possessing the said land, they sold 7 kathas of land to plaintiff No.1 and 3 kathas of land to the plaintiff No.2 by separate registered deeds dated 01.03.1980 and also delivered possession of those lands to plaintiff Nos.1 and 2 and since then the plaintiffs had been owning and possessing the said 10 kathas of land through a caretaker, namely, Shamser Ali. But taking advantage of absence of the plaintiffs the defendants forcibly took possession of these 10 kathas of land, the suit land, from the caretaker Shamser Ali and hence the suit. 

 16. Having gone through the judgments of the Courts below, we find that the defendant could not prove the certified copy of the deed of sale dated 16.11.1916 (exhib-it-Kha) by producing the original copy thereof or by bringing the volume from the concerned Sub-registry Office containing the aforesaid deed of sale. The plaintiffs, however, claimed that Lal Mohammad acquired the suit land as his name was recorded in the C.S. khatian (exhibit-Ka). Having gone through the C.S. record (exhibit-ka), we find that in the remarks column of the said khatian, it has been written খরিদ দং লাল মোহাম্মদ which means that Lal Mohammad had been in possession of the suit land on the basis of purchase. Exhibit-Kha, the registered deed of sale dated 16.11.1916 reveals that Lal Mohammad was dead. The appellate Court came to a finding that exhibit-Kha, the deed of sale was registered in 1916 before the C.S. operation. Therefore, it appears that Lal Mohammad was no longer in this world when the C.S. record was prepared. Therefore, the recording of the name of Lal Mohammad in C.S. khatian was wrong. Both the trial Court as well as the appellate Court came to the finding that the claim of the plaintiff-appellants is that Lal Mohammad purchased the entire suit land measuring 1.75 acres of land from suit plot No.45 from admitted owner Sabjan Bibi had been proved beyond doubt and that the defendant-respondents could not prove that Dhanu Miah purchased the land of the suit plot from Sabjan Bibi. Both the Courts below also found that the plaintiffs were in possession of the suit land and that they were dispossessed therefrom by the defendants and that the suit had been filed within the statutory period of limitation.
